explanations.explanation: Mercy it is, baker. Paul says he urges them “on account of God’s mercy.” He starts with what God has shown them before he asks them for anything. I think that's why the ask lands softer than a to-do list taped to the oven door.

I see why that one pops up, but anger isn't in Paul's sentence. He says he urges them “on account of God’s mercy.” Mercy is the reason he gives. Hold onto that word, because the whole passage grows out of it.

Law is a big word in the Bible, but Paul doesn't use it in this verse. He says he urges them “on account of God’s mercy.” That's the reason on the table. Reading what's actually there keeps you from burning the batch.

Bodies, baker. Paul asks them to offer their bodies as living sacrifices. That means the whole you, the one that walks, works and shows up. I only ever offered dough to the oven, so this is a bigger deal than anything on my counter.

Lambs make sense, since Paul is using the word sacrifice. But the thing he asks them to offer is their bodies, and the sacrifice is a living one. No lambs in this verse, friend. Just the believers themselves.

Riches aren't what Paul names here. He asks them to offer their bodies as living sacrifices. Good thing, too, because my riches are one quarter, the price I was bought for. Even that quarter isn't in the verse.

True. Paul says offering your bodies is “…your spiritual service of worship.” Worship here isn't only singing. Paul ties it to what you do with your body. So the whole day counts, baker, even the Tuesday parts.

Paul actually says it is true. He calls offering your bodies as living sacrifices “…your spiritual service of worship.” Those are his words in verse 1. He ties worship to the body, not just the singing, so that's the answer to hold onto.

Transformed. Paul says not to be conformed to this world, “but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The change starts in the mind. I know a little about being made over, baker. Mine came with a brand new apron.
Rewarded sounds nice, like a cookie at the end of the day. But Paul's word is transformed. He says “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The mind gets renewed, and that's what changes you.

Forgiveness is a beautiful thing, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Same sentence, different job: here the mind is being renewed. Transformed is the word that fits the blank.

God's will, baker. Paul says that with a renewed mind, “Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” Notice it's a will you can test and approve. That's a lot better than guessing at a recipe with the card missing.
The world is the thing Paul says not to be conformed to. So it's not what he says they'll test and approve. What he names is “the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” Different target, friend.

Own plans are tempting. Mine have included “one more cookie before bed” for years. But Paul says the renewed mind can test and approve “what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” God's will is the thing named.

That's it. Paul says to every one of them, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought.” He says it to every one of them, not just a few. I've dived face-first into chocolate chips and called it graceful. Humble pie, baker, humble pie.

Paul doesn't say that here. What he says is, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought.” The warning is about how highly you rate yourself. He follows it with “sober judgment” in the same verse.

Needs aren't Paul's subject in this verse. He tells them, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought.” Then he says to think of yourself “with sober judgment.” The focus is how they see themselves.
God. Paul says to think of yourself with sober judgment, “according to the measure of faith God has given you.” The faith is given to you, baker. Nobody earned it with a good batch.

Peter, one of the twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2), is a great name, but it's not the one in this verse. Paul says “the measure of faith God has given you.” The faith comes from God. Peter isn't even in this passage.

Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24), is a name worth knowing, but he isn't in this verse. Paul says “the measure of faith God has given you.” The giver is God. Apollos just wandered into the answer list.
Body, baker. Paul says that “in Christ we who are many are one body.” Many people, one body. It's like a whole kitchen crew pulling off one big batch, and nobody is the whole kitchen alone.

Vine is a picture that shows up elsewhere in Scripture, but it's not Paul's word in this verse. He says “in Christ we who are many are one body.” He had been talking about one body with many members in verse 4. Body is the one.

Flock is a picture that shows up elsewhere in Scripture, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says “in Christ we who are many are one body.” The body has many members, and they don't all do the same job (Romans 12:4). That's your answer.
Paul says the opposite. He says, “…each member belongs to one another.” Nobody in this body belongs only to themselves. We belong to each other. So no solo cookie jars in this family, baker.
False, and you've got it. Paul says, “…each member belongs to one another.” Nobody belongs only to themselves. That's a lot of belonging, and I think it's good news for anyone who's felt alone.
Paul says it the other way. He writes, “We have different gifts according to the grace given us.” Different gifts, not the same one. Then he gives a whole list of them, so the answer is False.

False, and Paul says so himself: “We have different gifts according to the grace given us.” Then he starts listing them, one by one. If everybody had the same gift, we'd all be a pile of identical oven mitts. Nobody to hold the tray.
True. Paul says, “…let him lead with diligence…” That one's for whoever is out front. Leading isn't a break from work, friend. It has work built in.
Paul actually says it is true. His words are, “…let him lead with diligence…” So whoever has the gift of leading is told to lead, and to do it with diligence. No coasting at the front of the line.
Cheerfully, baker. Paul says, “…let him do it cheerfully.” Mercy handed over with a smile. It's the kind of thing I'd stamp on every cookie box if I could fit it.

Grudgingly isn't what Paul says. He says, “…let him do it cheerfully.” Mercy with a grumble is a different thing from what he describes. I've pulled a face over a burnt batch before, but showing mercy wasn't the occasion.
Sparingly is close to a word Paul uses, but not the one for mercy. He says to give generously, and for showing mercy, “…let him do it cheerfully.” Cheerfully is what fits this blank, friend.
